The manipulation of time in the story is very well-balanced and enhances its quiet, atmospheric tone. The narrative covers roughly forty minutes of story time—from shortly before 7:00 AM to just after 7:30 AM. The author appropriately compresses the uneventful waiting periods at the dock into brief transitions while letting the arrivals and dialogues with the three passengers play out in near real-time to establish Ilse's grounded, stoic character. 

Later, during the short ferry crossing, time is subtly stretched when Ilse's phone rings. By slowing down the pacing during the few seconds the phone vibrates—lingering on the brightness of the screen, her thoughts of Jonas in Munich, the memory of the paper coffee cup, and the "angry trembling" of the device on the metal surface—the author effectively creates a moment of quiet emotional tension and hints at a deeper backstory without disrupting the understated rhythm of the piece.
